newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: INTERVIEW-Philippine's SEC wants Chinese walls.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Philippine's SEC wants Chinese walls.

text.p: The Philippine Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) vowed on Wednesday it would soon implement rules and reforms to ensure a more transparent equities market including the establishment of "Chinese walls."

As the market has grown and government liberalisation taen root, so an increasing number of players have taken on multiple roles which can lead to insider trading, SEC Chairman Perfecto Yasay told Reuters in an interview.
For instance, he said universal banks are authorised to act as underwriters, investment banks and stock brokers.

"We do not have the control system or safeguards that will prevent the spillover of confidential or proprietary information from one activity to another. This kind of a situation really encourages or makes one susceptible to insider trading activities," he said.

"We are certainly very much concerned about reports of price manipulation and rumour mongering so we have required brokers to verify first any rumour, and failure to do that he can be held liable for losses," said Yasay.

The Philippine stock market has recently been hammered by a wave of rumours of impending property collapses and bank failures, which some senior government officials contend amounted to outright manipulation.

One recent rumour, subsequently denied, was that foreigners would be allowed to buy A shares, normally the preserve of locals, which sent the prices plunging of blue chip B shares, which foreigners can purchase.
"We continue to maintain that foreigners cannot own A shares unless there is a Congressional effort to change the nationalistic provisions of our constitution," Yasay said.

The SEC chief said he hopes the Philippine Stock Exchange would be able to set in place procedures that will discipline members violating rules and evolve a scheme to provide a more equitable distribution shares in initial public offerings (IPOs)
"We hope to democratise the rules of the exchange because at present brokers get to keep their allocation when the IPO is hot and aggressively sell them when its cold," Yasay said.
Yasay said he is also pushing for the development of market specialists like large commercial banks who will be able to act as market makers for IPOs.
At present, Yasay said issuers illegally set up "war chests" to support price of their shares.
Yasay said these proposed reforms would be discussed with the Exchange, the Bankers Association of the Philippines and the Investments Houses Association of the Philippines.

Granting of a permanent self-regulatory status to the bourse, Yasay said, will depend largely on the implementation of these reforms. The Exchange's temporary self-regulatory status expired in February and has not been renewed by the SEC.
"The Philippine Stock Exchange will get its self-regulatory status as sure as the sun is rising tomorrow, but they will have to comply with these measures," Yasay said.
